title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Closed-Loop Evaluation** (Vol IV). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

A robot that repeatedly opens one door has supplied evidence about that door, its own hardware, and the conditions of those trials. It has not established how it will behave at a displaced latch, with a different payload, or after its sensors drift, and a flawless record from a short campaign remains consistent with a policy that fails a substantial fraction of its attempts.

rows: **Closed-loop estimand**

A physical success rate is the expectation of a frozen outcome predicate over a declared distribution of trial conditions (initial state, environment, unit, frozen policy and permission parameters), so it belongs to that population and to no other.
**Outcome channels and censored trials**
Task completion, proposer autonomy, and supervisory burden are separate channels, and an intervened run is an autonomy failure, never a success that was cut short (the censored trial fallacy).
**Offline evaluation illusion**
Replay resets the input to the recorded state each step, so a heading bias with a tiny angular MSE can spend a 15 cm aisle clearance in seconds once the loop closes.
**Four evidence regimes**

Replay, closed-loop simulation, shadow operation, and constrained physical testing sit on two axes (causal feedback, physical realism) and each trades one distortion for another, so they are not a fidelity ladder.
**Predeclared trial protocol**
A finite record supports a claim only if the target ODD, its weights, approximately independent draws, a frozen predicate, and the full denominator are fixed before the first run.
**Zero-failure bound**

At zero failures the Wald interval collapses, so a clean record is inverted exactly (failure bound about 3/n), which makes twenty clean runs consistent with a one-in-seven failure rate and makes every added nine cost about ten times the trials.
**Exposure wall**
Hazards are rates per operating hour, and bounding a rate lambda with zero events needs about 3/lambda failure-free hours, so rare hazards cannot be demonstrated by sampling the proposer.
**Evaluation record**

The evaluation record binds a bounded claim to its target ODD, configuration digests, sampling protocol, complete outcome log, exact statistics, and the catalog of unsupported gaps, which become runtime obligations.
**Simulator screening validity**
A simulator earns authority to screen candidates only through a paired sim-and-real benchmark scored for rank inversions, and even then it filters, never certifies.
**Sequential and comparative tests**
Early acceptance is valid only under a boundary declared in advance (Wald's SPRT), and comparing two checkpoints needs interleaved, randomized, blinded runs on one unit.
**Trajectory confinement**

Shadow operation runs the candidate on the real machine while the baseline keeps authority, so the candidate's inputs stay confined to the baseline's state distribution and its recovery is never tested.
**Runtime monitor channels**
Coverage gaps the record cannot close become five runtime monitor channels (input support, latency and freshness, constraint margin, intervention rate, environmental assumption).
